
## The mortality burden is larger than most clinicians assume

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
- Approximately **6.5 million** people develop an immediately life-threatening fungal disease each year,
  with **3.8 million** deaths, of which about **2.5 million (68%)** are directly attributable to the
  fungal disease itself [@denning2024burden].
- The single largest contribution to those deaths comes from cases that are never diagnosed, and therefore
  never treated [@denning2024burden].
- Mortality is concentrated in a few syndromes: invasive aspergillosis, *Candida* bloodstream
  infection, cryptococcal meningitis, *Pneumocystis* pneumonia and chronic pulmonary aspergillosis
  [@denning2024burden; @bongomin2017global]. In the United States alone, fungal disease accounts for
  substantial excess hospitalisation and cost [@rayens2022mortality].
- The at-risk population is expanding faster than the therapeutic armamentarium — transplantation,
  targeted immunotherapy, critical care, and advanced HIV disease in settings with limited diagnostics.
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {.keypoint}
**Case fatality, not incidence, is the problem.** For most invasive mould disease, 42-day
mortality remains 20–50% even with guideline therapy. Improvement will come from earlier diagnosis
and from agents that reach the infected compartment — not from more of the same mechanism.
:::

::: {.pearl}
Fungal disease is also a **resistance** problem with an agricultural driver: azole fungicide use selects
environmental resistance in *Aspergillus fumigatus* before any patient is exposed to a medical triazole
[@snelders2008tr34; @fisher2022threats].
:::
:::
:::

## WHO fungal priority pathogens list (2022)

| Priority | Pathogens | Why they are listed |
|---|---|---|
| **Critical** | *Cryptococcus neoformans*, *Candida auris*, *Aspergillus fumigatus*, *Candida albicans* | High mortality, rising resistance, diagnostic gaps, inadequate treatment options |
| **High** | *Nakaseomyces glabratus* (*C. glabrata*), *Histoplasma* spp., eumycetoma agents, Mucorales, *Fusarium* spp., *Candida tropicalis*, *Candida parapsilosis* | Resistance, limited access to therapy, high burden in specific regions |
| **Medium** | *Scedosporium* spp., *Lomentospora prolificans*, *Coccidioides* spp., *Pichia kudriavzevii* (*C. krusei*), *Cryptococcus gattii*, *Talaromyces marneffei*, *Pneumocystis jirovecii*, *Paracoccidioides* spp. | Intrinsic multiresistance or geographically concentrated burden |

::: {.keypoint}
The list is a **research and development agenda**, not a treatment guideline. Its practical message for
pharmacology: the pathogens with the worst outcomes are precisely those for which our existing classes have
either no activity (*L. prolificans*, *Fusarium*) or unreliable activity (*C. auris*, azole-resistant *A. fumigatus*)
[@fisher2022threats; @gow2022importance].
:::

## Why antifungal development is hard

- **Target scarcity.** Fungi are eukaryotes. Pathways that are essential are usually conserved with the host;
  selectivity must come from fungus-specific enzymes (Erg11, Fks1/2, Gwt1, fungal DHODH) or fungus-specific
  sterols and cell wall polymers.
- **Static versus cidal.** Only the polyenes are reliably fungicidal against yeasts *and* moulds; azoles are
  fungistatic against yeasts and fungicidal against moulds; echinocandins are the reverse.
- **Sanctuary sites.** CNS, eye, urine and necrotic/abscessed tissue are poorly served by the large, highly
  protein-bound molecules that otherwise behave well.
- **Trial design.** Mortality endpoints in heterogeneous, critically ill populations require large samples;
  the rarest and most resistant infections are studied in single-arm salvage trials.

Ibrexafungerp (2021), oteseconazole (2022) and rezafungin (2023) ended a long drought; fosmanogepix, olorofim
and opelconazole are in phase 2/3 [@hoenigl2021pipeline; @hoenigl2024novel].
:::
